universe_context:
Sanae Takaichi was elected prime minister of Japan by the National Diet on Tuesday, October 21, 2025, becoming the first woman to hold the office in the country’s constitutional history and Japan’s 104th prime minister. Takaichi, 64, is president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party and represents Nara Prefecture in the House of Representatives. A hardline conservative, longtime ally of the late former prime minister Shinzo Abe and admirer of former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, she entered office at a moment of political instability, public frustration over rising prices and weakened support for the LDP.

Her election followed the resignation of Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba and his cabinet earlier the same day. Ishiba, who had taken office on October 1, 2024, announced in September 2025 that he would step down after the LDP suffered damaging election losses. Under his leadership, the LDP-led coalition lost its majority in the House of Representatives in October 2024 and then lost its majority in the House of Councillors in July 2025. The party was also under pressure from public anger over a political fundraising scandal. At an extraordinary cabinet meeting shortly before 9 a.m. on October 21, Ishiba’s ministers submitted their resignations, formally clearing the way for the Diet to choose his successor.

Takaichi had won the LDP presidency on October 4, 2025, after defeating four male rivals in the party leadership contest. In the final round she defeated Shinjiro Koizumi, a former environment minister and son of former prime minister Junichiro Koizumi. Her victory marked a shift to the right for the traditionally center-right LDP. Takaichi had previously run for the party leadership in 2021 and 2024 without success. She had served in several senior roles before becoming party leader, including minister for internal affairs and communications, minister for economic security from 2022 to 2024, and other cabinet and vice-ministerial posts. She first won election to the House of Representatives in 1993 as an independent and joined the LDP in 1996.

Her path to the premiership became uncertain shortly after she won the LDP leadership because Komeito, the LDP’s coalition partner for 26 years, withdrew from the alliance. Komeito, a more moderate and pacifist party, cited dissatisfaction with the LDP’s response to political funding scandals. Its leader, Tetsuo Saito, also raised concerns about Takaichi’s views on wartime history, visits to Yasukuni Shrine and hardline positions toward foreigners, but said the decisive issue was the LDP’s insufficient response on political money reform. The breakup threatened the LDP’s hold on power because the party no longer had a majority in either house of parliament.

Takaichi secured enough support when the LDP reached a last-minute coalition agreement on Monday, October 20, with the Japan Innovation Party, also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai or Ishin. The party is based in Osaka and led by Osaka Governor Hirofumi Yoshimura, with Fumitake Fujita serving as a parliamentary leader. Ishin shares several policy positions with Takaichi and the LDP, including support for stronger defense, constitutional revision and a more hardline approach to national security and immigration. Takaichi said the two parties had “many common views” and were “essentially heading in the same direction.” The agreement included policy priorities such as economic measures, political reform, social security changes, a reduction in parliamentary seats and Ishin’s proposal to designate Osaka as a “secondary capital” alongside Tokyo. Ishin chose not to take ministerial posts in Takaichi’s cabinet at the start of the coalition, instead supporting the government from outside the cabinet.

In the House of Representatives vote on October 21, Takaichi won 237 votes in the 465-seat lower chamber, four more than the 233 needed for a majority. Yoshihiko Noda, leader of the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan, the largest opposition party, received 149 votes. Other votes went to Democratic Party for the People leader Yuichiro Tamaki, Komeito leader Tetsuo Saito and other candidates. In the House of Councillors, no candidate secured a majority on the first ballot. Takaichi received 123 votes, one short of the required 124, and Noda received 44. A runoff was held between Takaichi and Noda, and Takaichi won with 125 votes to Noda’s 46. After the lower house result was announced, Takaichi stood and bowed deeply as lawmakers applauded.

The new LDP-Ishin coalition still did not command a majority in either chamber, leaving Takaichi dependent on cooperation from other opposition lawmakers to pass legislation and to control key parliamentary committees. LDP Secretary General Shunichi Suzuki said the government’s immediate priority would be tackling rising prices and other economic measures, and he apologized for the delay caused by internal party wrangling after the July election. Takaichi also faced pressure to quickly prepare a major policy speech, compile economy-boosting measures by late December and manage foreign-policy engagements, including an expected early meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump.

Later on October 21, Takaichi moved to form her cabinet after the formal imperial investiture process. She appointed Minoru Kihara as chief cabinet secretary, Toshimitsu Motegi as foreign minister, Shinjiro Koizumi as defense minister and Yoshimasa Hayashi as internal affairs and communications minister. Satsuki Katayama became finance minister, the first woman to hold that post in Japan, and Kimi Onoda became economic security minister. They were the only two women in the cabinet apart from Takaichi herself. During her leadership campaign, Takaichi had said she wanted female representation in cabinet not particularly lower than Nordic countries, but women made up only a small share of the new lineup. Yoko Otsuka, a professor of welfare policy and gender studies at Ritsumeikan University, said that a female prime minister might slightly improve Japan’s Global Gender Gap Index ranking, “but the reality barely changes.”

Takaichi used her first press conference to emphasize economic revival and the U.S. alliance. “I am determined to deliver results for the nation, to build a strong Japan, and to never give up,” she said. She added that she planned to meet President Trump at an early date “to elevate the Japan-U.S. relationship to new heights.” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated her on becoming prime minister and said he looked forward to working with her to strengthen the India-Japan Special Strategic and Global Partnership, which he described as important for peace, stability and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific.

Takaichi’s election was celebrated as a historic breakthrough for women in Japanese politics, where women remain underrepresented, but her own views drew mixed reactions. She opposes same-sex marriage, supports the male-only imperial succession and opposes allowing married couples to use separate surnames. She has advocated stronger defense capabilities and revision of Japan’s pacifist constitution, aligning herself with Abe’s political legacy. South Korea was expected to watch her government warily because of her nationalist positions, while her hawkish stance toward China placed regional security high on her agenda. Domestically, her administration began with the challenge of restoring trust in the LDP, controlling inflation, managing a fragile coalition and proving that Japan’s first female prime minister could provide stable government after years of rapid leadership turnover.
key_facts: Sanae Takaichi was elected prime minister of Japan by the National Diet on October 21, 2025.
Sanae Takaichi became the first woman to serve as prime minister in Japan’s constitutional history and Japan’s 104th prime minister.
Takaichi was president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party and represented Nara Prefecture in the House of Representatives when she became prime minister.
Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba and his cabinet resigned on October 21, 2025, clearing the way for the Diet to choose his successor.
Ishiba announced in September 2025 that he would step down after the LDP-led coalition lost its House of Representatives majority in October 2024 and its House of Councillors majority in July 2025.
Takaichi won the LDP presidency on October 4, 2025, after defeating Shinjiro Koizumi in the final round of the party leadership contest.
Komeito withdrew from its 26-year coalition with the LDP after Takaichi won the LDP leadership, citing dissatisfaction with the LDP’s response to political funding scandals.
The LDP reached a coalition agreement with the Japan Innovation Party on October 20, 2025, allowing Takaichi to secure enough support to become prime minister.
The Japan Innovation Party supported Takaichi’s government from outside the cabinet and did not take ministerial posts at the start of the coalition.
Takaichi won 237 votes in the 465-seat House of Representatives, exceeding the 233 votes needed for a majority.
Takaichi won the House of Councillors runoff against Yoshihiko Noda by 125 votes to 46 after no candidate secured a majority on the first ballot.
The new LDP-Ishin coalition did not hold a majority in either chamber of the National Diet, leaving Takaichi dependent on cooperation from other lawmakers to pass legislation.

Takaichi appointed Minoru Kihara as chief cabinet secretary, Toshimitsu Motegi as foreign minister, Shinjiro Koizumi as defense minister and Yoshimasa Hayashi as internal affairs and communications minister.
Satsuki Katayama became Japan’s first female finance minister in Takaichi’s cabinet, and Kimi Onoda became economic security minister.
Takaichi’s stated early priorities included economic revival, responding to rising prices, strengthening the Japan-U.S. alliance and arranging an early meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump.

Takaichi is a hardline conservative who opposes same-sex marriage, supports male-only imperial succession, opposes separate surnames for married couples, supports stronger defense capabilities and advocates revision of Japan’s pacifist constitution.
